items.title: Rosa Parks was a trained activist, not a tired seamstress
items.claim: Rosa Parks's December 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat is often told as a spontaneous act. What was her actual background?

options.text: She had no prior political involvement and acted purely on impulse
She was secretary of the Montgomery NAACP and had attended training at the Highlander Folk School months earlier
She was a paid organiser sent specifically to provoke an arrest
She was a member of the Communist Party, which is why she was arrested

items.reveal:
Parks had been Montgomery NAACP secretary since 1943. In summer 1955 she attended a workshop at Highlander Folk School in Tennessee on desegregation strategy. She was also not the first to refuse — Claudette Colvin had done the same in March 1955 but was 15, pregnant, and considered unsuitable as a test case by the NAACP.

Parks later wrote: 'People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.'
items.why: The 'tired seamstress' story makes civil rights feel like an accident of individual virtue. The actual story is one of organised, strategic activism — which is harder to teach but truer.

items.title: The Terror killed around 17,000 by guillotine — and many more by other means
items.claim: What was the human cost of the French Revolutionary Terror (September 1793-July 1794)?

options.text: Around 17,000 official executions (16,594 verified by Donald Greer), plus tens of thousands killed in the Vendée civil war and many more dying in prisons

items.reveal:
Donald Greer's 1935 study 'The Incidence of the Terror' counted 16,594 official executions. The Vendée counter-revolution and its suppression killed perhaps 170,000-250,000. Around 200,000 were imprisoned during the Terror; thousands died in custody.

Robespierre fell on 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794) and was guillotined the next day — the wave he had ridden turned. The guillotine had been adopted in 1792 as a humane, egalitarian execution method.

The Bourbon Restoration (1814) and Napoleon III's regime committed their own political killings; the Paris Commune's suppression (1871) killed perhaps 10,000-20,000 in a week.
items.why: Death tolls determine how a revolution is remembered. The Terror's official 17,000 was orders of magnitude smaller than the Vendée suppression — but the urban, named victims shape memory.

items.title: Enclosure transferred millions of acres to private hands
items.claim: How much land was affected by Parliamentary enclosure (c. 1750-1850)?

options.text: Around 7 million acres — roughly a fifth of England — was enclosed by some 4,000 individual Acts of Parliament between 1750 and 1850
Enclosure was rare and ended in the 16th century

items.reveal:
Earlier enclosure (16th-17th centuries) had been informal and contested (Kett's Rebellion 1549). Parliamentary enclosure required individual Acts, with commissioners surveying and reallocating land in compact private holdings.

Common rights to graze, gather wood, glean and forage were extinguished. J. L. and Barbara Hammond's 'The Village Labourer' (1911) emphasised dispossession; later historians (J. M. Neeson, 'Commoners' 1993) revived the case for serious social impact.

The General Enclosure Acts of 1801 and 1845 streamlined the process. By 1900 the English commons were almost gone — though the Commons Preservation Society (1865) saved spaces like Hampstead Heath and Epping Forest.
items.why: The transition to industrial capitalism had a rural component. Enclosure freed up labour for cities and consolidated land for improved farming — at the cost of displacing a way of life that contemporaries actually missed.
